name: Goias
summary_text: Goiás stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling transphobia is punishable on the same footing as racism. Same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationally, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.  Lethal violence against trans people remains a documented feature of the national picture. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, recorded 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, with Brazil ranked first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Goiás accounted for 5 of those 80 national victims. Against a state population of roughly 7.2 million, that is a rate of about 0.69 per million per year, close to 1.8 times the national rate derived from the same year's figures.  The prior year's tally was higher: ANTRA's dossier for 2024, reported on 27 January 2025, recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders.  Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed in Brazil, including in Goiás. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.  Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes. Courts have also applied anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.  The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

name: Mato Grosso
summary_text: Mato Grosso stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and the 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism under constitutional and federal criminal provisions. The age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. Entry, visa and gender-marker rules operate on the same footing for trans visitors as for anyone else, a position confirmed by an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 covering same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules nationwide.  Detention carries a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where arrested or imprisoned LGBTI people are housed. Recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. The place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Violence against trans and travesti people remains documented at national scale. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, released on 26 January 2026, records 80 murders of trans and travesti people across Brazil in 2025, 34 per cent below 2024, alongside at least 75 attempted homicides marked by excessive violence. Mato Grosso accounted for 3 of those killings in 2025, placing the state 12th among Brazilian states, and has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017.  Within Mato Grosso, a jury has explicitly recognised the gender dimension of a trans woman's killing. On 16 April 2026, businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla, found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside the MT-485 highway in Sorriso, together with procedural fraud and corpse concealment. The jury held that the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.  The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.
